findings.title: Blind SQL injection via unquoted numeric interpolation bypassing mysqli_real_escape_string
findings.description: The untrusted input `$_POST['id']` (line 5) is escaped with `mysqli_real_escape_string` (line 11) and then interpolated directly into a SQL query **without surrounding quotes** on line 16: `"SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users WHERE user_id = $id;"`. `mysqli_real_escape_string` only escapes characters meaningful inside *quoted* string literals (single quotes, double quotes, backslashes, NUL). Since `$id` is placed unquoted in the query, an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL tokens (operators, keywords, subqueries) without ever needing a quote character. The application then differentiates output based solely on whether rows are returned (`$exists` boolean on line 24), making this a boolean-based blind SQL injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends POST data `Submit=1&id=1 OR 1=1` and observes "User ID exists in the database." They then send `Submit=1&id=1 AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE user_id=1)='a'`, iterating characters to extract the admin password hash one character at a time via the binary exists/missing response. No quotes appear in the injected `$id` portion that would be stripped by `mysqli_real_escape_string` — the outer single quotes around 'a' are inside the *existing* SQL string context, not in the PHP string, but to be safe the attacker can use hex/char equivalents like `CHAR(97)` to avoid all quotes entirely.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries instead of string interpolation. Replace the query construction with: `$stmt = $GLOBALS["___mysqli_ston"]->prepare("SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users WHERE user_id = ?"); $stmt->bind_param("i", $id); $stmt->execute();`. This correctly separates code from data regardless of quoting.

findings.title: Blind SQL injection in SQLite path with no input escaping at all
findings.description: When `$_DVWA['SQLI_DB']` is `SQLITE`, the raw value of `$_POST['id']` (line 5) is interpolated directly into the SQL query on line 35 with **zero escaping**: `"SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users WHERE user_id = $id;"`. Unlike the MySQL branch, there is no call to any escaping function. The result is used only as a boolean (`$exists` on line 37-38) to differentiate two response messages, making this a textbook boolean-based blind SQL injection with no filtering whatsoever.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends POST data `Submit=1&id=0 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users LIMIT 1`. If a row is returned, the response says "User ID exists in the database." For blind extraction: `id=1 AND SUBSTR((SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1),1,1)='a'` — iterated over all characters to exfiltrate the entire password hash.
findings.recommendation: Use SQLite prepared statements: `$stmt = $sqlite_db_connection->prepare("SELECT first_name, last_name FROM users WHERE user_id = ?"); $stmt->bindValue(1, $id, SQLITE3_INTEGER); $results = $stmt->execute();`.

findings.title: Stored XSS via malicious filename reflected into HTML without encoding
findings.description:
The user-controlled filename `$_FILES['uploaded']['name']` flows through `basename()` (line 5) into `$target_path`, which is later interpolated directly into an HTML string on line 24: `$html .= "
{$target_path} succesfully uploaded!
";`. `basename()` strips path separators but does NOT sanitize HTML. An attacker can set the filename to something like `.jpg`. This passes the extension check (last segment after dot is "jpg"), passes `getimagesize()` if a valid tiny JPEG body is provided, and the resulting path is rendered unescaped in the response.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker crafts a valid JPEG file smaller than 100KB. They set the upload filename to `.jpg` via a multipart request with a modified `Content-Disposition` filename parameter. The file passes all three validation checks (extension=.jpg, size<100000, valid image header). On success, the response HTML contains `
…/uploads/.jpg succesfully uploaded!
`, executing JavaScript in the victim's browser session. Because the message may be rendered on page reload or visible to admins reviewing uploads, this is stored XSS.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode `$target_path` with `htmlspecialchars($target_path, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before embedding it in output, or use a template engine that auto-escapes. Additionally, generate a random filename server-side rather than preserving the user-supplied name.

findings.title: Unrestricted file upload allows arbitrary PHP file upload leading to RCE
findings.description: The code performs no validation whatsoever on the uploaded file's extension, MIME type, or contents. An attacker-controlled filename from `$_FILES['uploaded']['name']` is passed through `basename()` (which only strips directory path components, not extensions) and used directly as the destination filename in `move_uploaded_file()` at line 10. While `basename()` prevents path traversal out of the uploads directory, it does not prevent uploading files with dangerous extensions such as `.php`, `.phtml`, or `.php5`. If the `hackable/uploads/` directory is accessible via the web server and PHP is configured to execute files in that directory, the uploaded file can be requested directly, achieving remote code execution.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uploads a file named `shell.php` containing `<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>` via the upload form. The file is written to `hackable/uploads/shell.php`. The attacker then sends a request to `http://target/hackable/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id` and receives the output of the `id` command, achieving full RCE on the server.
findings.recommendation: Validate the uploaded file extension against a strict whitelist of allowed extensions (e.g., `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`). Verify the MIME type independently using `finfo_file()`. Store uploaded files with server-generated names (not the user-supplied filename). Ensure the uploads directory does not allow script execution (e.g., via `.htaccess` `php_flag engine off` or Nginx `location` deny).

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized filename in upload success message
findings.description: At line 13, the variable `$target_path` is embedded directly into HTML output without HTML-encoding. `$target_path` contains `basename($_FILES['uploaded']['name'])`, which is attacker-controlled. The `basename()` function strips directory path components but does not strip or encode HTML special characters. A filename such as `<script>alert(1)</script>.txt` will be rendered as-is inside the `<pre>` tag, causing the browser to execute the script. The XSS fires in the browser of the user performing the upload (or a victim tricked into uploading via CSRF).
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker crafts a multipart request with the filename field set to `.jpg`. After the upload completes, the server responds with HTML containing the injected payload inside the `
` tag. When the victim's browser renders this, their session cookies are exfiltrated to the attacker's server.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode `$target_path` before embedding it in output using `htmlspecialchars($target_path, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Additionally, apply validation on the filename beyond what `basename()` provides.

findings.title: Unrestricted file upload via client-controlled MIME type bypass
findings.description: The code validates uploads by checking `$_FILES['uploaded']['type']` (line 9), which is the Content-Type header supplied by the client in the multipart HTTP request — entirely attacker-controlled. There is NO server-side content inspection (e.g., `getimagesize()`, magic bytes) and NO file-extension validation. As long as the attacker sets the MIME type to `image/jpeg` or `image/png` (line 14) and keeps the size under 100000 bytes (line 15), any file is accepted. The original filename (including extension) is preserved via `basename()` on line 7 and written to a web-accessible directory by `move_uploaded_file()` on line 18. An attacker uploads a `.php` file (e.g., a webshell) with a spoofed Content-Type header. The server-side check passes, the file is stored as `shell.php` under `hackable/uploads/`, and is directly executable via HTTP request.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a multipart POST request with a file named `shell.php` containing `<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>`, but sets the Content-Type of that part to `image/jpeg`. The MIME-type check on line 14 passes. The file is written to `hackable/uploads/shell.php`. The attacker then requests `hackable/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id` and gets arbitrary command execution on the server.
findings.recommendation: Validate the file extension against an explicit whitelist (e.g., only `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`). Independently verify file content server-side using `getimagesize()` or finfo. Store uploads outside the webroot or configure the upload directory to disallow script execution. Rename uploaded files to random names without preserving the original extension.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via uploaded filename interpolated into HTML
findings.description:
On line 22, the successfully uploaded file path is interpolated directly into HTML without encoding: `$html .= "
{$target_path} succesfully uploaded!
";`. `$target_path` (line 7) contains `basename($_FILES['uploaded']['name'])`, which is the original user-supplied filename. An attacker can craft a filename containing HTML/JavaScript (e.g., `.jpeg`). Because the upload check (line 14) only validates the client-controlled MIME type, the attacker simultaneously sets Content-Type to `image/jpeg`, causing the upload to succeed and the malicious filename to be rendered in the response HTML.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a multipart upload request where the filename field is set to `.jpeg` and Content-Type is `image/jpeg`. The file passes the MIME check, the upload succeeds, and line 22 renders the malicious filename as live HTML in the page, executing JavaScript in the victim's browser context and exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the filename before embedding it in output using `htmlspecialchars($target_path, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Additionally, apply basename validation or renaming to alphanumeric-only characters.

findings.title: Session cookie derived from predictable monotonic counter via md5
findings.description: On each POST request, the application generates the "dvwaSession" cookie value by taking the MD5 hash of a server-side counter (`$_SESSION['last_session_id_high']`) that starts at 0 and increments by exactly 1 on every request (lines 7-10). The cookie value is therefore always one of { md5(1), md5(2), md5(3), … }. MD5 is a deterministic hash, not a source of entropy — it merely obfuscates an entirely predictable input. An attacker can precompute md5(n) for all plausible n values (even millions fit in a trivial lookup table) and enumerate valid session tokens.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker precomputes a table mapping md5(1)..md5(100000) to their integer inputs. They observe that the application uses the "dvwaSession" cookie for authentication or authorization decisions. They set their own dvwaSession cookie to md5(1) (c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b), then md5(2), etc., until they find a value that maps to an active authenticated session — hijacking that user's identity.
findings.recommendation: Generate the session token with a cryptographically secure random source: e.g., `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`. Never derive session identifiers from deterministic or low-entropy values such as counters or timestamps.

findings.title: Predictable sequential session identifier enables session hijacking
findings.description: The cookie "dvwaSession" is set to a simple sequential integer stored in $_SESSION['last_session_id'] (line 6–10). Each POST request increments the counter by one (line 9), and that integer is emitted directly as the session cookie value (line 10–11). There is no entropy source — the token is fully deterministic and trivially guessable. An attacker who receives cookie value N knows every other valid session is a nearby integer.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a session and observes their dvwaSession cookie is, e.g., 42.
